evidence.quote: extends 161 miles (259 km) from Fairbanks to Circle, a town on the Yukon River

evidence.claim: A mining road from Fairbanks to Circle on the Yukon
evidence.quote: It was built to service the Circle Mining District

evidence.claim: The Steese Highway runs from Fairbanks to Circle on the Yukon River, with much of the road narrow and winding.
evidence.quote: extends 161 miles (259 km) from Fairbanks to Circle, a town on the Yukon River

evidence.claim: The Steese Highway runs from Fairbanks to Circle on the Yukon River, with much of the road narrow and winding.
evidence.quote: Much of it is narrow and winding.

evidence.claim: Alaska’s scenic-byways program highlights the Chatanika River, access to the White Mountains National Recreation Area and the midnight sun at Eagle Summit at summer solstice.
evidence.quote: Unforgettable sites, vistas and natural wonders along the route include the midnight sun at summer solstice, the Chatanika River and Circle Hot Springs.

evidence.claim: Alaska’s scenic-byways program highlights the Chatanika River, access to the White Mountains National Recreation Area and the midnight sun at Eagle Summit at summer solstice.
evidence.quote: The White Mountains National Recreation Area and Birch Creek National Wild & Scenic River are accessible from the Steese Highway.

evidence.claim: Alaska’s scenic-byways program highlights the Chatanika River, access to the White Mountains National Recreation Area and the midnight sun at Eagle Summit at summer solstice.
evidence.quote: Take in the midnight sun at summer solstice (June 21) at Eagle Summit.

evidence.claim: The full highway extends 161 miles from Fairbanks to Circle, ending about 50 miles south of the Arctic Circle.
evidence.quote: extends 161 miles (259 km) from Fairbanks to Circle, a town on the Yukon River about 50 miles (80 km) south of the Arctic Circle.

evidence.claim: The road was built to serve the Circle Mining District, productive in the 1890s before gold discoveries in the Klondike.
evidence.quote: It was built to service the Circle Mining District, which was very productive in the 1890s, before the discovery of gold in the Klondike.

evidence.claim: Completed in 1927, it took the name of General James G. Steese, a former Alaska Road Commission president.
evidence.quote: The highway was completed in 1927 and is named for U.S. Army General James G. Steese, a former president of the Alaska Road Commission.

evidence.claim: Mining remains part of its roadside story: the preserved camp at Chatanika and active dredging operations line the route.
evidence.quote: the preserved gold camp at Chatanika, and active dredging operations line the road.

evidence.claim: The Chatanika camp was built in 1925 by the Fairbanks Exploration Company, which also dug the Davidson Ditch to supply water to its dredges.
evidence.quote: The camp was built in 1925 by the Fairbanks Exploration Company (FEC), which also dug the nearby Davidson Ditch to supply water for the operation of the gold dredges.

evidence.claim: Leaving Fairbanks, the highway follows Alaska Route 2 to Fox, then Route 6 for most of the remaining journey.
evidence.quote: The Steese Highway is numbered Alaska Route 6 for most of its length, except for the first 11 miles (17 km) from Fairbanks to Fox, which are numbered Alaska Route 2.

evidence.claim: Gold Dredge Number 8 stands on the old Steese between Fairbanks and Fox.
evidence.quote: It is located on the old Steese Highway between Fairbanks and Fox

evidence.claim: Beyond Chatanika, Central’s museum interprets mining and displays mammal remains from Mammoth Creek.
evidence.quote: View pre-glacial Alaskan mammal remains found in Mammoth Creek at the Circle District Historical Society museum in Central.

evidence.claim: Beyond Chatanika, Central’s museum interprets mining and displays mammal remains from Mammoth Creek.
evidence.quote: The museum also offers a history of mining in the area.

evidence.claim: Circle ends the drive beside the Yukon, where river freight once supplied the gold camps.
evidence.quote: Circle is 160 mi (260 km) northeast of Fairbanks at the end of the Steese Highway along the Yukon River.

evidence.claim: Circle ends the drive beside the Yukon, where river freight once supplied the gold camps.
evidence.quote: it served as an unloading point for supplies shipped up the Yukon River from the Bering Sea. The goods were sent overland to gold mining camps.

evidence.claim: Five decks and a length of 250 feet give Gold Dredge Number 8 the scale of an industrial operation.
evidence.quote: Tour the 5-deck, 250-foot-long Gold Dredge Number 8

evidence.claim: The Fairbanks Exploration Company operated this ladder dredge from 1928 to 1959 on the old Steese Highway between Fairbanks and Fox.
evidence.quote: Goldstream Dredge No. 8 is a ladder dredge operated by the Fairbanks Exploration Company from 1928 to 1959. It is located on the old Steese Highway between Fairbanks and Fox

evidence.claim: Beginning in the 1920s, the 90-mile Davidson Ditch brought water into the area for mining.
evidence.quote: Starting in the 1920s, water was brought to the area through the 90-mile (145 km) Davidson Ditch for gold mining.

evidence.claim: The dredge cut a 4.5-mile track.
evidence.quote: The Goldstream Dredge No. 8 cut a 4.5-mile (7.2 km) track

evidence.claim: Its later recognition included National Register listing as a historic district in 1984 and designation as a Historic Mechanical Engineering Landmark in 1986.
evidence.quote: The dredge was named a Historic Mechanical Engineering Landmark by the American Society of Mechanical Engineers in 1986. In 1984, it was listed as a historic district on the National Register of Historic Places.

evidence.claim: Alaska’s transportation department includes tours of the dredge among its byway highlights.
evidence.quote: Tour the 5-deck, 250-foot-long Gold Dredge Number 8

evidence.claim: Central’s Circle District Historical Society museum pairs mining history with remains of pre-glacial Alaskan mammals found in Mammoth Creek.
evidence.quote: View pre-glacial Alaskan mammal remains found in Mammoth Creek at the Circle District Historical Society museum in Central.

evidence.claim: Central’s Circle District Historical Society museum pairs mining history with remains of pre-glacial Alaskan mammals found in Mammoth Creek.
evidence.quote: The museum also offers a history of mining in the area.

evidence.claim: Alaska’s transportation department identifies Central with one of the state’s most active mining districts.
evidence.quote: This town is one of the most active mining districts in the state.

evidence.claim: The Steese Highway passes through town.
evidence.quote: The Steese Highway (Alaska Route 6) does pass through Central.

evidence.claim: Circle began as a transfer point between river freight and inland gold camps.
evidence.quote: it served as an unloading point for supplies shipped up the Yukon River from the Bering Sea. The goods were sent overland to gold mining camps.

evidence.claim: Established in 1893 after gold was discovered in Birch Creek, it received supplies shipped up the Yukon from the Bering Sea.
evidence.quote: Circle was established in 1893 when gold was discovered in Birch Creek; it served as an unloading point for supplies shipped up the Yukon River from the Bering Sea.

evidence.claim: By 1896 it was the Yukon’s largest mining town, with 700 residents.
evidence.quote: In 1896, before the Klondike Gold Rush, Circle was the largest mining town on the Yukon River and had a population of 700.

evidence.claim: Gold discoveries in the Klondike in 1897 and Nome in 1899 drew away much of that population.
evidence.quote: Circle lost much of its population after gold discoveries in the Klondike in 1897, and Nome in 1899.

evidence.claim: The name outlasted a geographical mistake: miners thought they had reached the Arctic Circle, which lies about 50 miles farther north.
evidence.quote: Circle was named by miners in the late 19th century who believed that the town was on the Arctic Circle, but the Arctic Circle is about 50 mi (80 km) north of Circle.

evidence.claim: Mining continues in the area into the twenty-first century.
evidence.quote: Mining in the area has continued into the 21st century.

evidence.claim: Check 511 Alaska before driving through to Circle; the highway has three possible road-closure barriers.
evidence.quote: There are three possible road closure barriers, so 511 Alaska should be checked before traveling its length to Circle Alaska.

flags: The cached highway article places the pavement change both after about 81 miles and around Central. Those descriptions cannot be reconciled from this cache; omitted the current precise pavement transition.

The highway article calls this a National Scenic Byway; the official cache establishes inclusion in Alaska’s scenic-byways program but does not corroborate national status. Used the program description without a national designation claim.
Dropped the current 7.5-million-ounce claim: the official page assigns production to the site, while the dredge article assigns it to the dredge. Scope remains unresolved.
Central is intentionally shorter than 90 words because relevant local historical evidence is limited. No live access or road-condition checks were possible.
